contentSummary: This subtopic provides insights in understanding political parties and how they operate. It further outlines how leaders are chosen and how political parties interact with citizens in society. Through this sub topic learner will learn how political parties provide a platform for citizens to participate in decision-making process. A political partyA political party is a group of citizens who organize themselves with a common value, ideas and a goal towards forming government. A political party represents an alternative government in a country. Political parties originate from different aspects of our communities.The following are some of the factors that lead to the formation of political parties: Ideological differences: disagreements over ideology, principles and policies can lead to the formation of new parties. Teaching Module3 Economic interests: disagreements over economic policies and interests can lead to party formation Charismatic leaders: individuals with persuasive and compelling attitudes can lead others in the formation of a political party Human nature (inborn differences): by nature, people differ in the way they understand and look at issues of life. Therefore, differences in opinion lead people to form political parties Religious and communal sentiments: some people form political parties according to their religious beliefs Regional and geographic interests: parties may form to represent the interests of specific regions or geographic areas. For example, in the United States of America, the Republican Party initially represented the interests of the Northern states, while the Democratic Party, the Southern states Social and cultural issues: parties may form around social and cultural issues such as slavery, civil rights or immigration Historical events and crises: major historical events such as wars, economic depressions or social unrest may lead to the formation of parties. Learning ActivitiesDifferentiating between ruling party and an opposition party Differences between the ruling and opposition partiesa. Ruling party The ruling party is the political party which governs a country after winning elections and holds the governing power. It forms the executive arm of government (cabinet) headed by the president which is responsible for policy formulation and implementation. In the legislature, the ruling party initiates laws through public bills in line with its vision and development goals as enshrined in the party manifesto. It mobilises citizens to support national initiatives and government programmes.b. Opposition party An opposition political party is any political party which is not in government but works to provide checks and balances on the ruling party. This is done by questioning the actions, policies and decisions of government in power. It ensures that the government remains answerable to the citizens by holding government accountable for its actions It provides a healthy democracy by ensuring that government is accountable, transparent and responsive to the needs of the citizens. It presents alternative policies and programmes for development purposes and stands as an alternative government. It educates the public on important national and international issues Opposition political parties raise public debates that in turn force government consider popular concerns in the interest of the public Learning ActivitiesOutlining the structure of a political party (National Executive Committee, Provincial Executive Committee, District Executive Committee, Constituency Committee, Sections and Branches) Functions of a political party Selection or nomination of political personal Formation of public policies Conducting and criticism of government Political education. International between people and government Development and maintenance of s sense of national unity Coordinating the branches of government Making it possible for the electorate to function in an organized and effective manner. Framing of political issue for the people Selection of candidates during elections Serving as agencies of civic education Parties develop a sense of national unity Formulate party policies They permit the electorate to function They seek to control government They minimize the crushes of economic interests for the demand of various economic groups find expressions in party platforms. Teaching Module7 Learning ActivitiesDramatising a political campaign activity (meeting) A political party campaign is a selling of political ideas to the public in order to win the support of the public. it involves the dissemination of political party message to the public through rallies, debates, door to door canvasing, social media engangements and town hall meetings every political party has rights to disseminate information about its policies and idiologies as a means towards winning people’s trust to gain the votes The History of Political Party System in ZambiaSince independence Zambia’s political party system has changed from multiparty to one party and back to multiparty as illustrated in the table below:Party SystemPeriod Major Political Parties Party in PowerMulti-Party System 1964 to1972 - United National Independence Party (UNIP)- African national Congress (ANC)- United Progressive Party (UPP)United National Independence Party (UNIP)One-Party System 1973 to 1991 United National Independence Party (UNIP) United National Independence Party (UNIP)Multi-Party System 1991 to Date - Movement for Multiparty De-mocracy (MMD)- United National Independence Party (UNIP)- Patriotic Front (PF)- United Party for National Devel-opment (UPND) MMD (1991 to 2011)PF (2011 to 2021)UPND (2021 to ...) contentSummary: Zambia operates through both Local and Central Government systems. Local government is normally the decentralised system where power to govern is given to local authorities or councils to provide certain services to the communities at district level. Here learners will be given an opportunity to acquire more knowledge and competencies concerning the past and present trends in local authorities in Zambia. Before independence, the British Colonial administration ruled through tradition-al leaders or native authorities. Native authorities assisted the colonial government in collecting taxes, issuing licences and presiding over civil cases. After independence, Zambia enacted the Local Government Act Number 69 of 1965 which created four types of councils; City Councils, Municipal Councils Township Councils and Rural Councils. In 1980, the Local government and Decentralisation Act was enacted which placed all council under the control of District Governors In 1991, the Local Government and Decentralisation Act of 1980 was amended creating the current three types of autonomous councils; City (for cities), Munic-ipal (For Provincial Headquarters and other big towns) and District Councils (for small towns or districts). The 2019 Local Government Act outlines the three main types of Local Councils based on the size and status of the area they govern. The three are City councils, Municipal Councils and Town Councils. Learning ActivitiesExamining the structure of the local councils (city council, municipal council and town council) Under the current Local Government Act, City and Municipal Councils are headed by Mayors while District Councils are administered by Council Chairpersons together with Ward Councillors as Decision Makers. The administrative functions of the City and Municipal Councils are placed under the Town Clerk while the Town Councils are under the Council Secretary working with Directors of various Departments. THE STRUCTURE OF LOCAL COUNCILSCOUNCIL TYPEPOLITICAL HEAD (For Decision Making) ADMINISTARTIVE HEAD (For Implementing Programmes)City Councils Mayor working with ward councillors Town Clerk working with Directors of Departments Municipal CouncilsMayor working with ward councillors Town Clerk working with Directors of DepartmentsTown Councils Council Chairperson working with ward councillors Council Secretary working with Directors of Departments Local councils perform the following functions: zMaking By-Laws zProviding clean and safe water to communities zProviding accommodation and allocating plots for development zEnsuring a clean environment and pollution control zAllocating land for and maintaining graveyards zAwarding trading licences to business persons Teaching Module19 zMaintaining township roads and streets zBuilding and maintaining trading places such as markets zProviding street lighting zControlling the movement of livestock to and from the district zControlling drainage and sewage disposal zCity and town planning zProviding recreation facilities such as swimming pools and play parks zCollecting various kinds of levies, rates and rentals zProviding health facilities and controlling epidemics in communities zProviding fire-fighting services zPromoting local tourism Learning ActivitiesIdentifying sources of revenue for Local Government To undertake daily operations, local councils need to raise enough revenue. The most common ways by which councils raise funds are: zBusiness levies from business persons in the district zGrants from government such as the Equalisation Fund zPersonal levies paid by workers annually to the council zIssuance of Trading Licences zLocal revenue raising measures through such means as barriers, lodges, land rates, animal and crop levy among others zConstituency Development Fund for service delivery to constituencies One of the key functions of the local councils is to ensure environmental care and sanitation. This is mostly done through the following means: Cleaning public surroundings Tree planting in designated areas Providing and managing toilets in public places Providing rubbish bins in public places Developing and managing dumpsites Sewer and drainage control Sweeping of public places Provision of clean water and sanitation Learning ActivitiesIdentifying institutions and organisations that care for the environment Learning Environmwent Setup: This activity can be conducted from the natural environment through visiting institutions Taking care of the environment is an important activity which cannot be left to the local authorities alone. Other institutions and organisations can contribute significantly towards environmental care. These may include the following: zZambia Environmental Management Agency (ZEMA) zLine Government Ministries zCivil Society (CSOs) involved in environmental Management zNone Governmental Organisations (NGOs) committed to environmental care zSchools zReligious bodies zHouseholds and Communities This subtopic highlights the roles played by traditional leaders in the governance of a country. Through this topic, learners will be made to understand the composition and functions of the House of Chiefs in Zambia. Traditional leadership has been at the core of Zambia’s governance from pre-colonial, colonial and post-colonial eras. In pre-colonial era, traditional leaders were the only known leaders in the Zambian societies. The colonial administration practiced indirect rule by using traditional leadership to govern societies. Currently Zambia has a total of 288 Chiefs who play a significant role in the governance of a nation. They influence and motivate their subjects to achieve common goals and maintain order and harmony in communities. Traditional leaders play various roles in their communities which in-clude: zproviding spiritual guidance to their subjects zto preside over cultural, judicial and administrative activities in the chiefdoms. zTo resolve conflict among subjects zTo spearhead economic and social development in the community. zTo provide advice to political and religious leaders in society. zThey lobby for and spearhead developmental projects for their chiefdoms zThey are custodians of traditional leadership, customs and traditional land in their chiefdoms Article 169 of the Constitution of Zambia provides that there is established a House of Chiefs which shall consist of five chiefs from each province, elected by the chiefs in a Province, as prescribed.According to Article 169 Clause 5 of the Constitution, the functions of the House of Chiefs are to:(a) consider and discuss a Bill relating to custom or tradition referred to it by the President, before the Bill is introduced into the National Assembly;(b) initiate, discuss and make recommendations to the National Assembly regarding socio-economic development in the province;(c) initiate, discuss and decide on matters relating to customary law and practice;(d) initiate, discuss and make recommendations to a local authority regarding the welfare of communities in a local authority;(e) make proposals on areas in customary law that require codification;(f) advise the Government on traditional and customary matters; and(g) perform other functions as prescribed. contentSummary: This sub topics introduces learners to the concept of Central Government. Learners will be able to understand what central government is all about and how it relates with local government. Creating Strong Relationships in School Teacher-Learner relationships can be strengthened through zShowing passion zHighlighting the good more than the bad side of individuals zCreating of a safe and supportive environment for learners by showing empathy and understanding Peer relationships among learners can be strengthened through: zCollaborative activities and projects zPromoting inclusivity and respect among learners zShowing empathy and conflict resolution Community-School Relationship can be strengthened through: Teaching Module27 zRegular communication zEstablishment of Parent Teacher Committees (PTCs) zParticipating in voluntary activities towards the wellbeing of the school zCelebrating school successes for learners and the school The Central Government is the highest level of government in any country. It consists of the three organs of government, The Executive, the Legislature and the Judiciary as illustrated below:GOVERNMENT ORGANRESPONSIBLE OFFICIALSRESPONSIBILITYExecutive (Cabinet and Civil Service) PresidentVice PresidentCabinet Ministers + civil servants zAdministration of the law and public policies (administration)Legislature (Parliament) Speaker Deputy SpeakersMembers of Parliament zLaw making (legislation) Judiciary (Court System) Chief JusticeDeputy Chief JusticeJudgesMagistrates zInterpretation of the law (adjudication) The three organs of the central government play distinct roles. The legislature makes the laws, the judiciary interpret the laws and the executives carries out and enforces the laws. In order to carry out the laws, central government makes use of the civil service through different ministries, departments and agencies. Specifically, central government plays the following functions: zSpearheading the provision of Social Services like education and health care zRaising public revenue zBuilding public infrastructure like roads, bridges, airports, railway etc zProviding national security and defence zDeveloping various public policies to solve public problems zCreating a conducive environment for development Teaching Module29 zCentral government uses a centralised approach to decision making. z Local Government employs a decentralised approach. zThe Central Government consists of the cabinet headed by the President to make the decisions on behalf of the entire nation. zIn the Local Government, the council, headed by the Mayor/Council Chairperson working with councillors, make decisions at district level. zWhile central government is the higher level of decision making, local government is the lower level but both aim at service delivery to the people. zA process of transferring decision-making powers from the central government to the local government is known as decentralisation. This is to ensure quick delivery of services and effective participation of people in governance at local level. zPolicies such as international relations, national defence and public finance can be handled by central government while such policies like environmental protection, health care, education and housing can be a preserve of the local government.
